kurz: Before a surface can get hotter than 100 °C, its water has to evaporate. That costs a lot of energy and time.
bild_im_kopf: Like a pot of water on the stove: however strong the flame, the water does not get hotter than 100 °C. All the energy goes into evaporating.
was_passiert: Water needs a great deal of energy to turn into steam. As long as a surface is wet, it therefore stays stuck at about 100 °C. Only once the water is gone does the temperature rise and browning or crispness begin. The steam needs a way out: if it cannot escape, it steams the neighbouring pieces.
warum_wichtig: Explains why drying, leaving space and heat make such a difference. It is the key behind crisp, brown and crust.
faustregeln: Whatever goes into the pan wet stays stuck at 100 °C for a long time and does not brown.
Steam has to be able to escape: space, no lid, a rack instead of a plate.

praxis.text: Soaked potatoes not dried: the water has to evaporate first, and the crust comes late.
The bubbling in the oil is water evaporating. When it calms down, the surface is almost dry.
A full pan can no longer evaporate the juice that runs out. The meat stews grey.
